    Latest Update: Even justices have regrets

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (170 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In June 2023, the court decided Students for Fair Admissions, Inc.
    • In a recent development, but the justices did not account for one thing, according to Brooklyn Law School Professor Yuvraj Joshi: O’Connor’s later misgivings about that statement.
    • Nora is an editorial assistant at SCOTUSblog, based in Washington, D.C.

    In June 2023, the court decided Students for Fair Admissions, Inc. v. University of North Carolina, holding that race-conscious admissions at Harvard and the University of North Carolina violated the Constitution. Chief Justice John Roberts’ majority opinion in the case, along with Justice Brett Kavanaugh’s concurrence, cited Justice Sandra Day O’Connor’s 2003 prediction in Grutter v. Bollinger that “25 years from now, the use of racial preferences will no longer be necessary to further” student body diversity.

    In a recent development, but the justices did not account for one thing, according to Brooklyn Law School Professor Yuvraj Joshi: O’Connor’s later misgivings about that statement. In interviews with her biographer after she left the court, O’Connor acknowledged that the 25-year figure “may have been a misjudgment.” When asked for a upcoming estimate, she replied, “[t]here’s no timetable. You just don’t know.”.

    Nora is an editorial assistant at SCOTUSblog, based in Washington, D.C.

    Recommended Citation: Nora Collins, Even justices have regrets, SCOTUSblog (Nov. 20, 2026, 9:30 AM), https://www.scotusblog.com/2026/11/even-justices-have-regrets/.

    BigLaw firms are increasingly hiring lawyers with in-house legal department experience. (Image from Shutterstock).

    BigLaw firms, hunting for senior-level talent as they try to expand client relationships, are increasingly hiring lawyers with in-house legal department experience.

    In a recent development, over the past five years, Am Law 200 law firms hired about 740 lawyers from in-house positions. These in-house lawyers began their careers in firms, according to a story by Law.com.

    Lawyers who have switched from firms to in-house and then back to firms are being calling “boomerangs” in the legal industry, according to a FirmProspects report this month.

    Firms’ increasing investment in artificial intelligence also has them searching for lateral partners who have an expertise in AI or are open to increasing their understanding and use of it, according to Law.com.

    #112935. Criminal law is constitutional law

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2344 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    Criminal law is constitutional law

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2344 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that with arguments over the Second Amendment and the Excessive Fines Clause on the near horizon, this column seeks to provide some tranquil and more generalized ideas – a moment of Thanksgiving holiday respite.
    • Winship – criminal law fundamentals are constitutional law.
    • Sources indicate that every criminal law class I have taught over 40 years, from 1L first semester through advanced criminal procedure or federal criminal law, has begun with the same case: 1970’s In re Winship.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that with arguments over the Second Amendment and the Excessive Fines Clause on the near horizon, this column seeks to provide some tranquil and more generalized ideas – a moment of Thanksgiving holiday respite. Whether you are a Supreme Court follower who usually shunts criminal law to the side, or an experienced criminal law reader who might enjoy some holiday dinner thoughts for your friends and family, this column seeks to demonstrate that much of criminal law is actually constitutional law – and perhaps show why that can be so interesting. To do so, I will scatter some examples from last term, drawn from my recently published Annual Review of the Supreme Court’s Term, Criminal Cases booklet. When explaining criminal law to your friends or just opining over Thanksgiving dinner, I’d like to show why your mantra should be “crim law is con law” and vice versa.

    Winship – criminal law fundamentals are constitutional law.

    Sources indicate that every criminal law class I have taught over 40 years, from 1L first semester through advanced criminal procedure or federal criminal law, has begun with the same case: 1970’s In re Winship. Even non-lawyers know from film and TV that the prosecution’s high burden for proof in a criminal case is beyond a reasonable doubt. But do they know that this is constitutionally required? And perhaps more interesting, that this standard is nowhere, textually, in that document?

    “[T]he Due Process Clause protects the accused against conviction except upon proof beyond reasonable doubt of every fact necessary to constitute the crime with which he is charged,” wrote Justice William Brennan Jr. for the Winship court. If only all Supreme Court decisions had such clear and succinct rule statements.

    But why is this the rule? It is not found either in the body of the Constitution or in the Bill of Rights, which was adopted soon after the Constitution and focused largely on criminal law protections. Winship‘s answer: because that standard “dates back at least from our early years as a Nation,” “[i]t is now accepted in common law jurisdictions,” it is expressed “in many opinions of this Court,” and it has “long been assumed” to be “constitutionally required.” Thus history, tradition, and precedent support it. Perhaps most fundamentally, a high standard of proof, harder to satisfy than in civil law cases, is essential to fundamental fairness for the public as well as individuals charged with crimes. It is “indispensable to command the respect and confidence of the community” as well as “every individual” exposed to imprisonment. Or, as Justice John Harlan II wrote in an influential concurrence, this standard is “bottomed on a fundamental value determination of our society that it is far worse to convict an innocent man than to let a guilty man go free.”.

    Industry observers note that thus, a fundamental premise of criminal law, Winship, is constitutional law too. Moreover, and just by the way, Winship demonstrates that the “incorporation” theory of the 14th Amendment’s Due Process Clause (that is, applying the Bill of Rights to the states) is not limited to concepts stated expressly in the Bill of Rights itself – as “proof beyond a reasonable doubt” is not. Critics of non-textual constitutional rights – like privacy, a right to travel, a right to refuse medical treatment (like mask wearing?), or even a right to terminate a pregnancy – must confront the application of their literalist theory to proof beyond a reasonable doubt, too. For this reason, I also teach Winship in every constitutional law class.

    There are almost no crimes mentioned in the Constitution.

    In a recent development, this sometimes surprises 1L students (and others). But the goal of the Constitution was to (re)describe a system of government, and form “a more perfect Union” after the prior Articles of Confederation had proved unsatisfactory. It was not to write a criminal code. The states were then (and still are) the primary forum for criminal law.

    According to recent reports, so the Constitution defines only one crime, treason (in Article III, section 3). It mentions a few others, like “Bribery” (in Article II, section 4) and “Breach of the Peace” with a general reference to “Felony” (in Article I, section 6). And of course the Impeachment Clause (Article II section 4) mentions “high Crimes and Misdemeanors,” without definition. Again, states were expected to take care of the substantive definition and application of virtually all criminal law. (However, as I explained some years ago, the First Congress in 1790 did enact over two dozen federal crimes.).

    Yet a large focus of the Bill of Rights is criminal procedure.

    Recent findings suggest that three years after the Constitution was drafted, the Bill of Rights focused on criminal law rights in at least four proposed amendments (the Fourth, Fifth, Sixth, and Eighth). I won’t list the multitude of rights captured there, but they form the bulk of all criminal procedure law school classes today. The right to be free from unreasonable governmental searches and compelled self-incrimination, and the rights to counsel, jury trials, and no cruel and unusual punishments – and much more – are all embodied in the Bill of Rights.

    In a recent development, one example from last term: in Villareal v. Texas, the court had to interpret the Sixth Amendment right to “Assistance of Counsel” to decide (unanimously) that a criminal trial judge can order that the defendant not discuss their ongoing testimony with their attorney during an overnight recess.

    Recent findings suggest that why was the Bill of Rights so focused on criminal procedure rights? It’s a fun question to ask students, or at the Thanksgiving table if things get slow. Sooner or later someone gives the soundbite answer: “because most of the constitution’s framers were crooks.” They were certainly guilty of treason – then and still today a capital (that is, death penalty) offense, as well as other crimes (violence, destruction of property, incitement, and more). Had the revolutionary Framers been captured by the government (the British) they likely would have been hung. Instead, during the course of the revolution, numbers had been tried in absentia, found guilty by officials (not juries), and had their houses searched and occupied by troops. Cruel and unusual torture had been inflicted on some captured compatriots. When constitutional ratifying conventions demanded a bill of rights, protections from unfair criminal processes were therefore topmost on the minds of many drafters (if not perhaps “the People” at the time).

    (Another aside: ask your lawyer friends to compare the content of civil procedure versus criminal procedure classes today. The latter full-semester course is almost entirely constitutional law – I used to call my own crim pro class “Con Law Three.” By contrast, civil procedure classes, also a full semester, focus largely on the nitty-gritty details of federal rules, only occasionally wandering into statutes or the Constitution.).

    Recent findings suggest that in addition to the four explicitly criminal-focused amendments, you might then add general constitutional ideas that are bound to capture some criminal law cases: the First, Second, Third, and Ninth Amendments. The First Amendment’s direction, that “Congress shall make no law” regarding (“respecting”) or abridging freedoms of religion, speech, and the press, is a constitutional law command against criminal laws as well as civil. So too is a protection of a right to keep and bear arms, and to not have government troops quartered in “any” house (not just your own).

    And then consider the “great generalities” of the Constitution.

    In his 1921 Storrs Lectures at Yale Law School (subsequently published as “The Nature of the Judicial Process”), future Supreme Court Justice (and then New York Court of Appeals Judge) Benjamin Cardozo discussed “the great generalities of the Constitution.” Among these, the Equal Protection and Due Process Clauses of the 14th Amendment are huge sources of criminal law doctrine. Just last term, for example, the procedural steps required to apply the Equal Protection Clause against racial (and other) bias in jury selection, and the idea that due process and judicial integrity requires a “miscarriage of justice” exception to guilty plea waivers, received focused Supreme Court attention (in Pitchford v. Cain and Hunter v. United States, respectively).

    Recent findings suggest that criminal law cases focused on the meaning and application of these broad constitutional requirements arise regularly almost every Supreme Court term. Indeed, as I advise my students every year (again I aspire to teach with a smile, not didactic cynicism): no matter what arguments you make on the defense side of a criminal case, always add the words “and in violation of due process” to preserve at least a thread of a constitutional argument that you may not even perceive at the moment.

    In addition to equal protection and due process, I (and others) would add the Ninth Amendment, which speaks of unspecified “rights … retained by the people.” Justices have sometimes suggested that the Ninth and Tenth Amendments state nothing but “truism[s],” while other Supreme Court decisions have relied (at least in part) on the Ninth. For some, invocation of the Ninth Amendment may provoke if not laughter (it having been referred to by one academic as a “constitutional jester”), then a distinctly conservative or “originalist” rejection. Yet other conservative scholars such as John Yoo and Calvin Massey (my late former colleague) have written expansively about it. As Randy Barnett has argued, the Ninth Amendment “means what it claims,” and is “a significant guarantee of individual liberty.” If that is so, then it is (or could be) another source of criminal law protection for criminal defendants.

    According to recent reports, for example, Griswold v. Connecticut recognized a constitutional right to privacy in the criminal law context, resting in part (and almost entirely for three justices) on the Ninth Amendment. Less controversially, perhaps, Chief Justice Warren Burger later invoked the amendment in the 1980 case of Richmond Newspapers v. Virginia to support an “unarticulated” constitutional right for the public (and the press) to attend criminal trials. And in 2000, even Justice Antonin Scalia agreed (in a solo dissent to Troxel v. Granville, a non-criminal case) that the Ninth Amendment recognizes unenumerated rights. When you tell your Thanksgiving dinner companions that criminal law is constitutional law, don’t forget the Ninth Amendment.

    So criminal law is, very often, constitutional law.

    Thus it should be unsurprising (as detailed in my Annual Review of the Supreme Court’s Term, Criminal Law booklet) that 22 of the court’s merits decisions last term that address criminal law involved elements of constitutional law (17 fully argued cases plus five summary (unargued) decisions). That’s a substantial percentage of the court’s entire merits opinions docket, roughly a quarter or more.

    Statutory criminal law cases also often involve constitutional law.

    Sources indicate that by now I hope that you are persuaded: criminal law is (often) constitutional law. “But wait – there’s more!” When you combine the Constitution’s Supremacy Clause with the oft-cited judicial doctrine of constitutional avoidance, criminal cases requiring statutory interpretation also fall into this category. That is, these are criminal law cases that involve consideration of constitutional law. Advocates in statutory cases often raise potential constitutional objections to a criminal statute or to its application in their case, or they may raise constitutional law ideas in favor of their preferred interpretation. In addition, an understanding of constitutional doctrine can be necessary to properly evaluate the merits of a statutory claim. The bottom line is that, in many statutory criminal cases, explication or consideration of constitutional law is necessary or helpful to explain the result.

    Just a few examples from last term: In Barrett v. United States, the court had to mine the details of double jeopardy doctrine to agree, unanimously, that a statute could be interpreted as not permitting two convictions for a single act, thereby avoiding a constitutional problem. In Olivier v. City of Brandon, the court had to examine Olivier’s constitutional claims in order to decide whether the federal civil rights statutes were a proper vehicle for him to sue under. And in Whitton v. Dixon, the court had to briefly explain the constitutional Giglio doctrine, regarding a prosecutor’s failure to disclose exculpatory impeachment information, to reverse an application of the federal habeas corpus statue.

    It has been revealed that immigration cases also often require constitutional law, either to dispose of the merits or to resolve statutory concerns in them. Last term’s birthright citizenship case, Trump v. Barbara, is the most obvious example. Because immigration and criminal law cases are often intertwined – consider recent ICE arrests, detentions, and criminal violation grounds for removal – I include them in my annual review as well as the purview of this column. And even civil cases that I consider related to criminal law often require consideration of constitutional law concepts. For example, last term’s Hencely v. Fluor Corp., rejecting a claim of government contractor immunity, required consideration of constitutional preemption doctrine.

    In other words, criminal law mixed with constitutional law is everywhere.

    Last week, many of us were focused on the details of elections around the country, major and small. And next week, after Thanksgiving, will be chock full of criminal law and related Supreme Court oral arguments. So I’ve tried to give you a break today, and provide a few thoughts that are, perhaps, entertaining, or provocative, or at least interesting ways to navigate your mealtime gatherings (rather than focusing on the usual subjects). For some of you, perhaps this column has simply demonstrated what you already considered obvious; or perhaps it has opened interesting linkages in your mind between constitutional law and criminal law. In any case, thanks for reading this far. Next week I hope you are fortunate enough to breathe relaxing breaths, give thanks, and dwell not on legal minutiae but on what really matters.

    Rory Little has been teaching Constitutional and Criminal Law topics at UC Law SF (formerly Hastings) for over 30 years, after 12 years of practice.

    Recommended Citation: Rory Little, Criminal law is constitutional law, SCOTUSblog (Nov. 20, 2026, 10:00 AM), https://www.scotusblog.com/2026/11/criminal-law-is-constitutional-law/.

    Chinese tech giant Huawei convicted of stealing trade secrets

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (306 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Abajournal

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • After four days of deliberations, a federal jury convicted the Chinese telecommunications giant Huawei of conspiring to steal trade secrets and evade U.S.
    • After four days of deliberations, a federal jury convicted the Chinese telecommunications giant Huawei of conspiring to steal trade secrets and evade U.S.
    • The jury delivered its verdict Tuesday following an 11-week trial in which prosecutors argued that the tech giant committed “crime after crime” to build its empire, Law.com reports.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    After four days of deliberations, a federal jury convicted the Chinese telecommunications giant Huawei of conspiring to steal trade secrets and evade U.S. sanctions on Iran. (Photo from Shutterstock).

    After four days of deliberations, a federal jury convicted the Chinese telecommunications giant Huawei of conspiring to steal trade secrets and evade U.S. sanctions on Iran.

    The jury delivered its verdict Tuesday following an 11-week trial in which prosecutors argued that the tech giant committed “crime after crime” to build its empire, Law.com reports.

    According to recent reports, the tech giant was found guilty of conspiring to steal trade secrets, commit wire and bank fraud, violate U.S. sanctions and launder money, as well as multiple fraud charges. In all, Huawei was found guilty of 10 out of the 12 counts tried by prosecutors at the U.S. attorney’s office for the Eastern District of Latest York.

    Recent findings suggest that “Few crimes are as serious as Huawei’s decades-long pattern of endangering U.S. national security, violating the sanctity of U.S. commerce, and impeding the enforcement of U.S. laws,” U.S. Attorney Joseph Nocella said in a statement. “Today’s verdict is a step towards accountability for Huawei’s criminal activities, which includes yearslong collaboration with sanctioned entities in Iran, repeated lies to banks, and blatant thefts from U.S. technology companies.”.

    Sources indicate that jurors, however, rejected the lead racketeering conspiracy charge, as well as one count of conspiring to obstruct justice. Defense attorney Brian Heberlig claimed that as a victory.

    “It’s hard not to have profoundly mixed emotions from the verdict we just heard, but the single lead charge that was brought by the United States government against Huawei was the RICO charge, a charge that alleged that the firm was corrupt from top to bottom,” Heberlig stated in a press conference immediately after the verdict was revealed.

    #112925. Breaking: The Supreme Court and profanity

    📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2204 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: The Supreme Court and profanity

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2204 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • on October 30, 1973, John Douglas was driving with his 15-year-old son when he heard a litany of profanity come over the radio.
    • The station later mentioned it had chosen Carlin’s routine because it was an “incisive satirical view of the subject under discussion,” in the style of other great satirists like Mark Twain or Mort Sahl.
    • Before playing the routine, the host had warned that it included language some listeners might find offensive and suggested they return in 15 minutes if they were inclined toward offense.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that around 2 p.m. on October 30, 1973, John Douglas was driving with his 15-year-old son when he heard a litany of profanity come over the radio. New York’s WBAI, a nonprofit radio station, was airing a program on modern attitudes toward language. Near the end, the station played George Carlin’s “Filthy Words” routine, which begins with the comedian saying he’d been thinking about “the words you couldn’t say on the public airwaves; the ones you definitely wouldn’t say, ever.” He went on to repeat those words several times, contrasting them with words like “bastards,” “hell,” and “damn,” which were mostly acceptable, and showing how even some of his list of seven were perfectly fine in other contexts. His point was to show the absurdity of profanity.

    The station later mentioned it had chosen Carlin’s routine because it was an “incisive satirical view of the subject under discussion,” in the style of other great satirists like Mark Twain or Mort Sahl. Carlin, the station explained, was doing more than “mouthing obscenities.” He was “using words to satirize as harmless and essentially silly our attitudes towards those words.”.

    Before playing the routine, the host had warned that it included language some listeners might find offensive and suggested they return in 15 minutes if they were inclined toward offense. But about a month later, John Douglas complained to the Federal Communications Commission about the transmission which he stated was “garbage” and had been broadcast in the presence of his “young son.” He was the only listener to do so. A member of Morality in Media who frequently listened to the station to “see how far” they’d go, Douglas later acknowledged that he had laughed out loud at the bit but “did not appreciate WBIA’s ‘smart-alecky’ on-air provocations.”.

    The previous year, Carlin had been arrested after performing an earlier version of the same routine, but a judge threw out the charge. This time, the FCC found the broadcast “indecent,” and put its order in the station’s license file.

    That order ended up before the Supreme Court.

    Industry observers note that early in its order, the FCC acknowledged that Congress had forbade it from censoring broadcasts. But Congress had also prohibited the broadcast of “obscene, indecent, or profane” language, and the Commission thought Carlin’s broadcast fit the bill. In the FCC’s view, the ban on “indecent” language covered not just obscenity, but also patently offensive language when there was a reasonable risk of children listening. Late at night, when children were unlikely to be listening, the same material might be okay if it appeared in a work of serious literary, artistic, political, or scientific value.

    Recent findings suggest that two commissioners thought even that was too permissive. Charlotte Reid believed “this language to be totally inappropriate for broadcast at anytime” and thought the commission’s standard did “not go far enough.” Commissioner James Quello took much the same view. “Garbage is garbage,” he wrote, whether children were listening or not.

    It has been revealed that the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit, however, set aside the order in a 2-1 vote, with one judge believing it violated the statutory ban on censorship and the other saying it violated the First Amendment. The FCC appealed to the Supreme Court.

    At oral argument, which was held in April of 1978, several justices made their distaste for Carlin’s bit plain. When Pacifica’s lawyer stressed that the station had warned listeners beforehand and aired the monologue as part of an educational program about language, Chief Justice Warren Burger incredulously asked, “This is educational in your view?” And when counsel defended the material’s artistic value, Justice Thurgood Marshall responded, “Well, I’m not an expert, but if that’s artistic, deliver me.” Justice William Rehnquist, for his part, tested the limits of Pacifica’s position with a hypothetical involving a single four-letter word repeated for an hour. Would the FCC be powerless to prohibit that? Justice John Paul Stevens, however, seemed troubled by the potential reach of the FCC’s position, given that the prohibition on indecency could be enforced through criminal law.

    One striking exchange concerned the Justice Department’s position to argue separately, and more narrowly, than the FCC. The solicitor general’s office urged that the First Amendment prevented the government from barring particular words outright for a substantial part of the day without regard to context, even if the FCC could constitutionally regulate “indecency” to some extent. Rehnquist sharply asked why the Justice Department was arguing against the FCC, what interest it had in seeking a narrow construction of an act of Congress, and whether the solicitor general, as the government’s lawyer, could ever argue that an act of Congress was unconstitutional.

    Justice Lewis Powell also pressed the DOJ on the reasons behind its departure from the FCC, noting that the DOJ had supported the FCC in the court below. “That is true, and that is an embarrassment to us,” Deputy Solicitor General Louis Claiborne acknowledged, suggesting it was because the matter had been handled there by the Antitrust Division rather than the Criminal Division. Another explanation, which he did not mention, was that the administration had changed.

    The court ultimately ruled 5-4 that the FCC could constitutionally treat this broadcast as “indecent” under the governing statute, and that the government could constitutionally prohibit indecency even though it fell short of legal obscenity. Stevens wrote for Burger, Justice Harry Blackmun, Powell, and Rehnquist, having apparently struggled with the case and flip-flopped before settling against Pacifica. The Commission had treated the piece as a nuisance, and, as the court had observed in Village of Euclid v. Ambler Realty Co., a nuisance could be as simple as “a pig in the parlor instead of the barnyard.” He concluded that “when the Commission finds that a pig has entered the parlor, the exercise of its regulatory power does not depend on proof that the pig is obscene.” Though the holding expanded the government’s power to regulate speech, Stevens emphasized broadcasting’s pervasive presence in the home and its accessibility to children, the fact the piece was broadcast during the daytime, and the narrowness of the holding. He did not address late night broadcasts or the “occasional expletive.”.

    Recent findings suggest that stevens had only three votes for some parts of his opinion. Powell, joined by Blackmun, wrote separately to object to Stevens’ suggestion that the level of protection that speech receives should depend on a judge’s perception of that speech’s value. For them, the combination of repeated, patently offensive language, an afternoon broadcast, and children’s ready access was enough to resolve the case. Powell also addressed the concern that the decision could end up “reduc[ing] the adult population . . . to [hearing] only what is fit for children”: adults could buy tapes or hear the same words at theaters.

    Justice Potter Stewart dissented, joined by Justices William Brennan, Byron White, and Marshall. Stewart would have resolved the case on statutory grounds. He read “indecent” to reach only obscene material, and everyone agreed that Carlin’s monologue fell outside that category. His opinion recalled his concurrence in Jacobellis v. Ohio, where he voted to overturn an obscenity conviction for showing a French film with an explicit love scene. Stewart understood obscenity narrowly, but declined to define it, famously observing in that case, “I know it when I see it, and the motion picture involved in this case is not that.”.

    Industry observers note that brennan wrote a separate dissent, joined by Marshall, that went further. He agreed with Stewart on the statute and mentioned he would ordinarily refrain from addressing the constitutional question, but he found “the Court’s misapplication of fundamental First Amendment principles so patent, and its attempt to impose its notions of propriety on the whole of the American people so misguided,” that he was “unable to remain silent.”.

    Brennan disputed the analogy between a radio broadcast and an intrusion into the home. Listeners voluntarily turn on the radio, and they can voluntarily turn it off. In perhaps his sharpest passage, he wrote:.

    Brennan also questioned the majority’s reliance on protecting children. He read the court’s precedents as allowing the government to shield children from material that was obscene as to them. In his view, Carlin’s routine fell outside that category. Keeping it off the radio during the afternoon cut off access for adults as well as children. And while the majority had invoked parents’ right to raise their children as they saw fit, Brennan thought the FCC had somewhat ironically made the choice for them.

    Industry observers note that finally, he remained unconvinced that the court’s reasoning would reach only cases like Carlin’s. Among the things it could sweep in were “literary works, novels, poems, and plays by the likes of Shakespeare, Joyce, Hemingway, Ben Jonson, Henry Fielding, Robert Burns, and Chaucer,” “a good deal of political speech, such as the Nixon tapes,” and even portions of the Bible. In his view, the public, and not the court, should have the power to weed out “worthless and offensive” speech in a marketplace “unsullied by the censor’s hand.”.

    According to recent reports, brennan and Marshall had joined together in another Supreme Court opinion involving the F-word. In Cohen v. California, they joined Justice John Harlan II’s opinion protecting the right to wear a jacket emblazoned with “Fuck the Draft.” Stewart joined it too (not surprisingly, Burger and Blackmun dissented). Brennan brought Cohen straight into his Pacifica dissent; as he made clear, changing the words can change what the speaker communicates, something that applies especially well to Carlin because the taboo words were themselves the subject of the routine. And Brennan thought telling listeners to buy a record or pay to see Carlin live missed what it meant to hear the routine on the radio.

    In closing, Brennan wrote that the majority had only “confirm[ed] Carlin’s prescience as a social commentator.” (It was interesting that Marshall, who sounded distinctly unimpressed by the claim of artistic merit at oral argument, joined him, perhaps especially here.) As Brennan pointed out, Carlin had made fun of the rules about which words you could say on the air, and the court had exemplified the very attitude he was satirizing. To top it all off: Appended to the opinion is the transcript of Carlin’s routine, giving his “indecent” words a permanent home in the U.S. Reports.

    According to recent reports, at the 2002 Billboard Music Awards on Fox, Cher dispatched the critics who’d spent decades predicting her downfall with “So f*** ’em.” At the 2003 awards, Nicole Richie asked whether anyone had tried getting cow manure out of a Prada purse, then used the F-word to describe how hard it was. The next year, after Bono called U2’s Golden Globe win “really, really f***ing brilliant,” the FCC announced that even a single expletive could be indecent, and it later applied that approach to the two earlier Fox broadcasts.

    It has been revealed that in 2009, the Supreme Court took up the dispute in FCC v. Fox Television Stations. Writing for a 5-4 majority, Justice Antonin Scalia held that the FCC had adequately explained its change in policy under the Administrative Procedure Act, leaving the First Amendment question open. Justice Clarence Thomas joined the majority but wrote separately to question Pacifica’s holding. On remand, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 2nd Circuit struck down the policy as unconstitutionally vague.

    The case returned to the Supreme Court in 2012 and all eight participating justices agreed on the result (Justice Sonia Sotomayor recused herself). Justice Anthony Kennedy’s opinion held that the FCC had failed to give Fox fair notice that fleeting expletives could trigger an indecency finding, but once again left both Pacifica and the First Amendment question open. Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg wrote separately to say that Pacifica was wrong from the start and deserved reconsideration. But while the court has had several cases involving curse words since, it has yet to take up the question directly.

    In 2004, the FCC dismissed complaints related to the airing of Saving Private Ryan on the basis that the film’s curse words helped convey the soldiers’ experience. But just two years later, it slapped a station with $15,000 in fines for airing a Martin Scorsese documentary about Blues music that contained profanity. In 2020, the FCC received over 1,300 complaints about Jennifer Lopez and Shakira’s halftime show, though it never took any action against the network. And in February 2026, FCC requested transcripts of Bad Bunny’s Superbowl halftime performance before ultimately finding no violation.

    Half a century after Carlin’s seven dirty words, the FCC’s continued and seemingly arbitrary application of its indecency laws shows the prescience of Brennan’s dissent and the need to finally answer the question of whether the Constitution prohibits the “dominant culture” from trying to force “groups who do not share its mores to conform to its way of acting, thinking, and speaking.”.

    Anastasia Boden is a Senior Attorney at the Pacific Legal Foundation, where she brings civil rights lawsuits that advance the Constitution’s promises of equality and economic opportunity.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, in September, Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson received an award named after the late Justice William Brennan, a liberal lion.
    • Recent findings suggest that since joining the court in the summer of 2022, Jackson has sought to promote her understanding of that view.
    • Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

    In a recent development, in September, Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson received an award named after the late Justice William Brennan, a liberal lion. In her acceptance speech, Jackson discussed Brennan’s role as the Supreme Court became more conservative, noting that he “believed that even his dissents could make a difference and remind the nation that the pursuit of equal justice under law is an ongoing effort.” Jackson indicated that she agreed with that idea, telling the audience that she saw “dissent[s] as more than just a disagreement with the outcome of a case, I see them as an expression of faith in the future and a demonstration of hope.” As she put it, “However desolate the moment feels, we who write for a future age have hope that the noble and collective work of bending the long arc of the law toward justice will continue.”.

    Recent findings suggest that since joining the court in the summer of 2022, Jackson has sought to promote her understanding of that view. Although she has been consistently part of the court’s liberal bloc, even among the three Democratic appointees she has forged a unique role. As her invocation of Brennan suggests, it often appears that her goal is not simply to express disagreement with the majority, but to offer an alternative vision and to speak to the public directly – even if she does so without the support of her fellow liberals.

    Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

    In the column, Moritz called upon the Ohio legislature to fix this by passing the Endowment Accountability Act, House Bill 751 and Senate Bill 368 by the end of December. The bill states that donors who believe a public university has violated an endowment agreement must first notify the state’s attorney general, who has 180 days to correct course. Donors in Ohio now have no clear way to hold public universities accountable.

    According to recent reports, A former head of Baker & Hostetler’s corporate practice and director of Cardinal Health, Michael Moritz attended Ohio State’s law school on a full-ride scholarship before graduating in 1958. Less than a year after making his donation, Moritz, 68, was killed by a hit-and-run driver in Naples, Florida.

    The Second Amendment and an "unusually dangerous" approach to dicta

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1817 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Please note that SCOTUS Outside Opinions constitute the views of outside contributors and do not reflect the opinions of SCOTUSblog or its staff.
    • On November 10, The Newly introduced York Times published an article suggesting that a major piece of the Supreme Court’s Second Amendment jurisprudence is premised on a misquote by the late Justice Antonin Scalia in his 2008 majority opinion in D.C v.
    • According to the Times piece, “[t]he consequences of Justice Scalia’s use of ‘and’ rather than ‘or’ have been profound”: “Since all guns are dangerous, courts have had to focus instead on determining whether a type of firearm is unusual, often parsing marketing data and consumer surveys to gauge a weapon’s popularity.” Presumably, if Scalia had used the phrase “dangerous or unusual,” it would be easier for legislatures to ban even certain commonly owned firearms because dangerousness alone would be sufficient to bring a category of weapons outside the amendment’s protective sphere.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Please note that SCOTUS Outside Opinions constitute the views of outside contributors and do not reflect the opinions of SCOTUSblog or its staff.

    On November 10, The Newly introduced York Times published an article suggesting that a major piece of the Supreme Court’s Second Amendment jurisprudence is premised on a misquote by the late Justice Antonin Scalia in his 2008 majority opinion in D.C v. Heller, in which the court held that there was an individual right to possess firearms. The essence of the piece is that Scalia used the phrase “dangerous and unusual” to describe those weapons not protected by the right to keep and bear arms, attributing this terminology primarily (or perhaps solely) to the 18th century British jurist William Blackstone. Yet Blackstone’s writings instead use the phrase “dangerous or unusual.”.

    According to the Times piece, “[t]he consequences of Justice Scalia’s use of ‘and’ rather than ‘or’ have been profound”: “Since all guns are dangerous, courts have had to focus instead on determining whether a type of firearm is unusual, often parsing marketing data and consumer surveys to gauge a weapon’s popularity.” Presumably, if Scalia had used the phrase “dangerous or unusual,” it would be easier for legislatures to ban even certain commonly owned firearms because dangerousness alone would be sufficient to bring a category of weapons outside the amendment’s protective sphere.

    According to recent reports, the Times story has reverberated rapidly, with strong backlash from conservative lawyers and scholars. Such disagreements have focused largely on the specific citation Scalia used. Law professor Jonathan Adler, for example, has argued that the citation to Blackstone was one among many, and additional sources that Scalia cited used the “and” formulation. Others have responded that Scalia was anything but sloppy, which would be especially true when it came to such an influential and important source.

    Both sides, though, seem to be burying the lede. In my view, this is a story not about historical errors or the nuances of legal citation. Rather, it is about how judicial dicta that was never intended to lay down broad, permanent rules has taken on a life of its own, and how other justices on the Supreme Court subsequently canonized Scalia’s stray language by turning it into a “test” that would govern any number of future cases – when it’s not at all clear Scalia ever contemplated this or would have endorsed any such thing.

    As most law students and lawyers are well aware, the holding-dicta distinction is deeply rooted in American jurisprudence: generally speaking, the holding is the analysis necessary to resolve the actual case before the court, and everything else in an opinion is dicta (this comes from the Latin phrase “obiter dictum,” or “said in passing”). Fundamental to that distinction is that dicta, while it may be persuasive, is not precedential. As Chief Justice John Marshall wrote in 1821, the reason for not deferring blindly to dicta is “obvious”:.

    The late Judge Richard Posner once similarly emphasized the risk that dicta “can be misleading if carelessly lifted from the case-specific contexts in which they were originally uttered … That is why courts in assessing the binding effect of previous decisions distinguish between the dicta, which are the inessential parts of the opinion, and the holding.” Circuits vary in their approach to Supreme Court dicta, generally deferring more heavily to such language when they find it thoroughly considered or supported, but the court is, of course, never bound by its own dicta.

    In fact, Scalia himself was no fan of relying heavily on dicta from prior Supreme Court decisions. In a 1993 opinion, he criticized a group of dissenting justices by noting that their position found “support, if at all, only in the dicta of this Court’s opinions.” This was, in Scalia’s view, as good as no support at all. Indeed, Scalia rejected reliance on “drive-by … rulings” not fully considered by the issuing court, even if not purely dicta. In his 2015 decision for the court in Kerry v. Din, Scalia excoriated a proposition advanced in a dissenting opinion as resting solely on “dictum in a footnote” and then observed that “[t]he footnoted dictum that Justice Breyer proposes to elevate to constitutional law is a dangerous doctrine.” He further joined opinions that rejected prior dicta as unprincipled, especially when greater investigation revealed reasons for caution.

    Scalia’s position was nuanced – for example, he once joined a dissent by Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg that endorsed reliance on certain dictum as persuasive – yet a cautious approach to dicta is consistent with his broader judicial philosophy as well. He was at times willing to jettison even precedential decisions squarely applicable to the case at hand when those decisions were contrary to original public meaning. Unconsidered dicta, presumably, would then be far lower in the pecking order.

    Returning to Heller and the phrase at matter, it’s hard to argue that the “dangerous and unusual” passage from Heller is anything but dicta. The issue in Heller was whether a Washington, D.C. ordinance “generally prohibit[ing] the possession of handguns” violated the Second Amendment, or if there was an individual right to keep arms for one’s self-defense. Scalia’s majority opinion answered in the affirmative, as “the American people have considered the handgun to be the quintessential self-defense weapon.” D.C. never argued that handguns were entirely exempt from protection because they were especially dangerous. The question of dangerous and/or unusual weapons was not at issue in the case; accordingly, it wasn’t thoroughly investigated through the adversarial process.

    Recent findings suggest that rather, after canvassing the historical evidence and concluding it supported an individual-rights view of the Second Amendment, Scalia turned to the nature of the right he had just explicated. In three short paragraphs not necessary to the holding, he explained why the amendment did not authorize gun keeping-and-carrying by anyone in any circumstance; rather history revealed limitations on the right, such as “the carrying of ‘dangerous and unusual weapons.’”.

    Whatever the purpose of this section – Justice John Paul Stevens later suggested the language was proposed by Justice Anthony Kennedy (the crucial fifth vote in Heller) in exchange for joining the majority – it was far from necessary to resolve the case at hand.

    So how did such dicta become relevant? In the 2016 case Caetano v. Massachusetts, decided after Scalia had passed away, the justices unanimously overturned a Massachusetts Supreme Court decision upholding that state’s ban on stun guns in a criminal prosecution of a woman who used this weapon to defend herself from an abusive ex-boyfriend. Justice Samuel Alito issued a concurring opinion (joined by Justice Clarence Thomas) that performed an interesting maneuver. Seizing on the fact that the per curiam opinion in that case referenced Scalia’s “dangerous and unusual” formulation, Alito turned Scalia’s language into a doctrinal test: “As the per curiam opinion recognizes, this is a conjunctive test: A weapon may not be banned unless it is both dangerous and unusual.” But the per curiam had done no such thing; rather, that opinion simply cited the passage in Heller as referring to one limitation on the right to keep and bear arms. And the per curiam said that the lower court in that case had faltered by concluding that any weapon not in common use in 1791 was per se unusual, not by failing to use a conjunctive test.

    (Ironically, Alito has his own well-publicized objections to giving past Supreme Court dicta undue veneration – his opinion for the court in Dobbs heavily suggested that Roe’s viability framework was entitled to less weight in the stare decisis analysis because it was initially mere dicta, “the Court’s own brainchild [for which n]either party advocated.”).

    Recent findings suggest that from there, the “dangerous and unusual” language took on a life of its own. In 2022’s New York State Rifle & Pistol Association v. Bruen, in which the court struck down New York’s concealed-carry law, the majority set forth a test for Second Amendment constitutionality privileging historical evidence above all else. At the first step of that test, a court determines whether the conduct at glitch is protected by the right to keep and bear arms, which is where the exclusion of dangerous and/or unusual weapons becomes relevant. If the banned weapon is not protected by the Second Amendment (for, say, being “dangerous and unusual”), a constitutional challenge is dead on arrival. If, on the other hand, the plaintiff can show the weapons are protected, then the burden switches to the government to provide historical evidence to support its regulation. (The consequences may be even greater, as some have argued that “usualness” (or “common use”) conclusively establishes not only threshold protection for the weapon but also that any legislative ban is ahistorical and thus unconstitutional.).

    In a recent development, this test has divided the judiciary in recent years. For example, a Massachusetts federal judge evaluating a challenge to that state’s AR-15 ban recognized the apparent disconnect between Heller and Blackstone but nevertheless noted that “the Supreme Court has expressly stated . . .that the relevant tradition is one of regulating ‘dangerous and unusual weapons.’” The Massachusetts judge found these weapons were not in “common use,” and, in any event, a historical tradition of responding to technological advances by regulating specific weapons supported the ban. By contrast, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 3rd Circuit interpreted Scalia’s language to signal that widespread ownership of AR-15s and large-capacity magazines meant any legislative attempt to ban them was unconstitutional. The “dangerous and unusual” framework has led other judges on a search for ownership statistics and sales data to assess a weapon’s popularity, triggering sharp debate over whether a test that ultimately turns on commonality is even workable.

    This is particularly relevant since the court is at the moment preparing to hear oral argument in Viramontes v. Cook County, a Second Amendment challenge to state and local bans on AR-15s, on December 2. While the recent attention to Scalia’s citation may trigger discussion at oral argument, most justices are now likely to treat “dangerous and unusual” as an established standard and ownership statistics as definitive proof that AR-15s are not unusual and thus protected. Absent from this, however, will be the fact that this standard did not emerge from any well-reasoned, litigation-tested analysis making it deserve deference in the first place – especially under Scalia’s own approach to judging.

    The debate over Scalia’s Blackstone citation, then, has obscured a more important problem: the Supreme Court’s decision to treat its past dicta as doctrine that can settle the outcome of cases on which the court has never passed.

    Andrew Willinger is an Assistant Professor at Georgia State University College of Law, where he teaches constitutional law and civil procedure.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The president has promised that the import taxes will bring back manufacturing jobs and reduce the federal deficit, but last year's tariffs contributed to higher inflation.

    WASHINGTON (AP) â President Donald Trump’s administration is planning to hike tariffs on Chinese goods by an additional 20% and raise import taxes on products from the European Union, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and nine other major trading partners.

    The upcoming tariffs proposed on Wednesday are meant to discourage excessive factory output in those economies, boosted by subsidies and other trade barriers that the Republican administration notes allow overseas companies to flood global markets with cheap goods and put American manufacturers at a disadvantage. The taxes are also intended to help replace the tariff revenues lost after the Supreme Court ruled in February that Trump could not declare an economic emergency to bypass Congress and impose across-the-board tariffs.

    The duties stem from investigations into the trade practices of 12 countries, the 27-member EU and the self-governing island of Taiwan.

    Industry observers note that U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said he did not expect the tariffs to rattle the global economy.

    Industry observers note that âWeâve talked to our trading partners about this â they know what weâre proposing,â Greer told CNBC. âI think a lot of this is baked in, and I donât think any of these would actually take effect earlier than a couple months from now.â.

    The tariffs, rolled out the day before Thanksgiving, demonstrate the Trump administration’s willingness to continue imposing tariffs even after voters in this month’s midterm elections punished Republicans by handing majorities in the House and the Senate to Democrats. About two-thirds of voters noted that Trump’s policies had made the economy worse, according to The AP Voter Poll, a sweeping survey of the American electorate conducted in all 50 states.

    Trump has promised that the import taxes will bring back manufacturing jobs and reduce the federal deficit, but last year’s tariffs contributed to higher inflation that angered voters and led to calls by Democratic lawmakers to require congressional approval going forward.

    Sources indicate that while many Democrats campaigned against tariffs, any effort to overturn them will face major challenges even after they take control of both chambers next year. Some Democrats will likely support some of the tariffs, particularly on China. And Trump can veto any legislation that seeks to overturn the import taxes.

    After roughly two years of seemingly arbitrary tariffs imposed on a range of trading partners from Canada and Europe to Brazil, the duties announced Wednesday reflect a key goal of Trump’s trade officials: Pushing back against subsidized factories overseas that can produce and export goods regardless of market conditions.

    At the same time, Ryan Majerus, a trade lawyer and former official in Trump’s first term who also served in the Biden administration, noted the Trump administration took steps â such as not stacking these duties on top of earlier tariffs imposed in July â to mitigate the impact on consumers.

    In a recent development, âThis is kind of their legacy tariffs,â Majerus mentioned. âThis is the one that most closely encapsulates what theyâre trying to do, while also having a degree of recognition of the midterm results of the angst over tariffs.â.

    The small business advocacy group We Pay the Tariffs, which urged Congress to roll back all tariffs after the election, slammed Wednesday’s maneuver.

    In a recent development, âThree weeks ago, voters unambiguously rejected tariffs that have worsened the affordability crisis and devastated small businesses,â Dan Anthony, executive director of the group, said in a prepared statement. âCustomers canât afford more price increases, but small businesses canât afford to absorb tariffs on top tariffs either.".

    The levies will be imposed pursuant to Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, which permits the president to impose import taxes and other sanctions against countries found to engage in unreasonable or discriminatory trade practices.

    A senior Trump administration official told reporters that the new tariffs would be consistent with the trade deals that Trump reached last year with dozens of countries after threatening severe tariff hikes.

    Brazil was separately singled out Wednesday for extra punishment after talks on trade issues stalled. The U.S. is proposing higher import taxes for raw and refined sugar and a new 10% tariff on aircraft, a move that would hit Embraer, Brazilâs largest aircraft maker.

    For some Chinese goods, the new 20% tariff will be stacked on top of other import taxes for a total rate of 45%.

    Vietnam also faces a 20% rate, pending finalization of trade talks, the USTR said on Wednesday. The tariffs for other trading partners range from 10% to 18%.

    Sources indicate that the U.S. and China last year reached a trade truce that is set to expire on Jan. 10, 2027. Greer told CNBC that the administration is proposing a âbroad exemptionâ for $30 billion worth of Chinese goods in line with the truce.

    Trump met last week in Shenzhen, China, with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and aims to host him next month at the Group of 20 summit in Florida, an event at which the truce and issues over access to rare earth minerals and China’s purchases of American agricultural products could be discussed again.

    On Wednesday, Chinaâs Ministry of Foreign Affairs again stated its opposition while calling for the U.S. to resolve the matter through dialogue. âA tariff war or a trade war serves no partyâs interests,â spokesperson Guo Jiakun noted.

    The new import taxes are targeted to specific products and would not stack on top of separate tariffs on automobiles, steel, aluminum and other products that the administration has separately imposed under Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962.

    Nor would they stack on top of levies of 10% to 12.5% declared in July for 60 trading partners that the White House mentioned have inadequately enforced bans on goods produced by forced labor.

    Other nations facing the newly introduced tariffs are Bangladesh, Cambodia, India, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland, Thailand and Vietnam. Two other countries face pending investigations: Mexico and Norway.

    The USTR posted extensive reports on each country’s alleged unfair trade practices, with the report on China reaching 456 pages. The Section 301 law requires specific analysis of each country’s trade practices to pass legal muster.

    Wednesday’s duties will likely face legal challenges, as Trump’s forced labor tariffs already have. At least some of the forced labor duties could be overturned, Majerus mentioned, because the USTR didn’t provide extensive evidence for each of the 60 countries affected by those duties.

    Recent findings suggest that the Associated Press confirmed the planned tariff announcement ahead of the call, according to people who insisted on anonymity because they were not authorized to comment publicly. The prepares were reported earlier on Tuesday by Bloomberg and The Wall Street Journal.

    Still, that effort can only succeed if the Second Circuit gives credence to the truckersâ claims that congestion pricing is unconstitutional and preempted by federal law, arguments that have already failed at the appellate level.

    U.S. Circuit Judge Maria Kahn, a Joe Biden appointee, acknowledged it was Congress that passed the Value Pricing Pilot Program â the program under which congestion pricing was created â in the first place.

    âDoesnât the fact that Congress created the VPPP, which led to the approval of the tolling program here, undermine your argument that Congress intended to preempt precisely this type of congestion pricing law?â the judge asked.

    Carr noted that wasnât necessarily the case. The VPPP established the framework to create novel strategies to manage highway congestion, but that doesnât mean every program envisioned under it is necessarily a lawful one.

    Recent findings suggest that âYes, Congress did approve it. No, this program does not pass constitutional muster,â he said.

    Carr added that this case was different from the others that challenged congestion pricing in the past. Other lawsuits have generally focused on the impact of passenger vehicles, while this one, as Kahn put it, hinges on a âvery unique fee structure imposed on trucks.â.

    Brandon Trice, representing the state agencies carrying out the tolling program, disagreed.

    Sources indicate that âI donât think thatâs a distinction,â he said, arguing that truckers pay more because their vehicles contribute most to traffic congestion â and also benefit most from reduced traffic. âAs we know, living in Latest York, trucks take up a lot of space when they turn, when they double park.â.

    It has been revealed that wednesdayâs three-judge panel, which also included U.S. Circuit Judges Amalya Lyle Kearse, a Jimmy Carter appointee, and Myrna PÃ©rez, a Joe Biden appointee, didnât immediately rule following the hearing.

    The case is one of several challenging congestion pricing, which has been in place since the start of 2025 and, based on data from its first year, has led to measurable drops in traffic and emissions in Latest York Cityâs central business district.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that this week, the country entered a technical recession and saw a decline in its creditworthiness. But the president stands by his program of making deep cuts and slashing inflation.

    BUENOS AIRES (CN) â The Argentine president pledged to turn his country into a first-world economy, with booming markets and consumption peaks. Anarcho-capitalism, he promised, would lead citizens to compete at their best, propelling growth for both individuals and the nation.

    Sources indicate that but on Tuesday, almost three years into his administration, President Javier Mileiâs economy entered a technical recession, with its financial risk among the highest in the world outside of active war zones or countries with prolonged defaults. Argentina trails only nations such as Venezuela, Ukraine, Lebanon and Sudan.

    Argentina â known for its currency caps and import restrictions before Milei’s arrival â has seen drastic social and financial changes over the past 36 months.

    Industry observers note that the libertarian government slashed public spending by nearly a third, lifted trade barriers and dismantled currency controls. While his administration has achieved a fiscal surplus and brought down annual inflation from triple digits to about 30%, public perception of his economic policies has dimmed amid a shrinking labor market and declining consumption.

    âItâs a tough moment,â said Chiche Savore, who owns a convenience store on the outskirts of Buenos Aires. âPeople buy much less; their pockets are tight.â.

    According to recent reports, savore, who has known his clientele for years, noted Argentina has become expensive for its citizens. Utility rates have skyrocketed. Fixed costs take up almost all of lower- and middle-class workers’ income.

    Recent studies show severe losses in purchasing power have driven a sharp rise in household indebtedness. According to a report this year by the University of Buenos Aires, the real purchasing power of Argentina’s minimum wage has fallen by 40% since Milei took office in December 2023. Official pension system data reveals over the same period, the country has shed more than 300,000 registered formal jobs, especially in manufacturing and construction.

    Recent findings suggest that this erosion of income has left 41% of households with children unable to cover their basic monthly expenses, according to a recent UNICEF survey. To bridge the gap, half of surveyed families now carry debt, primarily to buy food and pay utility bills. Credit card borrowing doubled from 16% to 32% of households in a single year. And it’s harder for people to repay their debt.

    Yet on Wednesday, hours after Argentinaâs official statistics institute declared the country had entered a âtechnical recessionâ â when a countryâs gross domestic product contracts for two consecutive quarters â Economy Minister Luis Caputo stated âpeople need to understand these policies have come to stay.â.

    Like Milei, who has repeatedly stressed his administration won’t soften its tough financial policies, Caputo mentioned recession was âbasically an arbitrary technical term.â It would be a mistake to focus on perceptions of the outcomes of the governmentâs policies, he said.

    In a speech earlier this month at Argentinaâs central bank, Milei similarly dismissed short-term quarterly contractions, insisting his broader program had expanded the economy âregardless of what may be happening over a couple of quarters, and whether or not a technical recession is recorded.â.

    MatÃ­as Wasserman, an economist at the Observatory of Economic Situation and Public Policies, said the governmentâs economic policy is failing on its own terms.

    Sources indicate that âThey wanted to reactivate economic activity, regain trust from the markets and, from there, walk a path of growth,â Wasserman said. âBut the countryâs risk index has surpassed 1,000 points.â.

    Compiled by JPMorgan, the index measures the extra yield investors demand to hold an emerging nationâs bonds over U.S. Treasury notes, with every 100 points representing 1 percentage point of additional interest. Surpassing 1,000 points effectively shuts Argentina out of international credit markets, complicating efforts to refinance upcoming debt maturities and driving up borrowing costs across the economy.

    Wasserman noted that the administration has oriented its entire economic, monetary and exchange-rate policy around lowering that metric to regain market access.

    Sources indicate that âI am optimistic that we are laying the foundations for the liberal golden century that will make Argentina great again,â Milei remarked in a recent interview. The president, who plans to run for a second term next year, maintains an approval rating in the mid-30% range.

    Lara Goyburu, head of consultancy group Management and Fit, mentioned 40% of voters would elect him again if they were to vote now.

    âDespite the worrying economic situation,â Goyburu noted, âthereâs no one challenging him.â.

    Milei won the 2023 election as a political outsider with little public track record, making his way into politics by building alliances with the countryâs more conservative right-wing parties. In an unprecedented turn for Argentina, he managed to govern for three years with little experience by relying on legislative deals in Congress and backing from the financial establishment.

    In a recent development, with Cristina Kirchner, the head of historic center-left movement Peronism, under house arrest and barred from running, the opposition is struggling to converge around a single candidate. A year ahead of the October election, it is unclear if that figure will ever emerge.

    âThereâs a lack of political alternative,â Goyburu mentioned. With the economic decline, Argentina’s future is hard to predict. âAnd the markets are taking note of the uncertainty,â she said.

    #112907. What do these Supreme Court plaintiffs have in common?

    📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 16m • 📚 Deep Dive (3137 w)
