    Press Forward gave $20 million to 205 local newsrooms over two years. Here’s how some of them spent it.

    📅 29 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 22 min read (4364 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Niemanlab

    ⏱️ ~22 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that all the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing.
    • Recent findings suggest that we have sent a confirmation link to .
    • The unrestricted funding helped small outlets plug holes and try new things, but publishers ran up against the limits of what two $50,000 grants could accomplish, especially when it came to hiring.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that all the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

    Nearly there — check your email.

    Recent findings suggest that we have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

    The unrestricted funding helped small outlets plug holes and try new things, but publishers ran up against the limits of what two $50,000 grants could accomplish, especially when it came to hiring.

    Most local newsrooms in the U.S. have one thing in common: They need more money, and many dream of dollars they can use however they want.

    Sources indicate that RELATED ARTICLEPress Forward awards $20 million to 205 small local newsroomsSophie CulpepperOctober 16, 2024In 2024, Press Forward, the nonprofit trying to mobilize a philanthropic army for local news, announced it would give at least 100 small local newsrooms — those with annual budgets under $1 million — just that type of unrestricted funding. Almost 1,000 newsrooms applied. Ultimately, Press Forward distributed $20 million to 205 outlets. Most of them received $100,000 each, split over two years.

    I wondered what the recipients had done with the money, and which problems it had (or hadn’t) solved. Between May and October, I spoke or emailed with more than 30 grantees.

    The grantees represented every U.S. state, came from cities, suburbs, and rural areas, and published in multiple languages. They included for-profits and nonprofits, print and digital-only publications, college newsrooms, and public radio stations. Statewide newsrooms with fully staffed teams like The Maine Monitor, scrappy news startups like 285 South, and community newspapers powered by freelancers and part-time staff like the Copper River Record in Alaska all received funding.

    Recent findings suggest that for many newsrooms, Press Forward was the first grant they’d ever applied for. “Many of the country’s newsrooms are small, and few get foundation grants,” mentioned Press Forward executive director Dale Anglin. The open call was designed to change that and to distribute the money rapidly. Grantees were required to complete two LION sustainability audits a year apart; Press Forward is analyzing that data now and will release its findings next month.1.

    RELATED ARTICLEA study of nonprofit newsrooms reveals some cracks in the model’s foundationSeth C. LewisOctober 6, 2026“People tell me that what Press Forward did was unusual and rare within philanthropy,” mentioned María José Ramírez Braiz, founder and CEO of Midwest-based grantee Te Lo Cuento News.

    It has been revealed that “They said to us at the beginning of the grant period, before the shit hit the fan with the federal government, ‘If you need this money to keep the lights on, keep the lights on,'” said Copper River Record editor Allison Sayer, one of the paper’s two part-time staffers. “I feel that this was really a gift.”.

    Industry observers note that first-time grant applicants and recipients, in particular, noted Press Forward’s recognition gave them credibility and visibility with other funders. And publishers described the funding as a morale boost that validated low-paid work.

    Sources indicate that “It has been a life-changer, a lifesaver for us,” mentioned Gretchen Sporleder Orr, who publishes the World Journal in southern Colorado with her husband. Her voice broke when she talked to me about the funding. “I don’t know if we would be in business right now if it wasn’t for the Press Forward money.”.

    The Real WV “would not still exist without Press Forward,” said Stephen Baldwin, the site’s volunteer publisher. (He’s also the former minority leader for the West Virginia Senate and a pastor of two churches.) The outlet was one of eight grantees that received just two $25,000 grants over two years. “There’s not exactly a lot of capital floating around West Virginia for nonprofit news,” Baldwin said, “and without this outside impact, we wouldn’t be able to do this work.” But he hopes that the site can be less reliant on grants in the future.

    Sources indicate that the funding did not save every recipient. One grantee, Atlanta Civic Circle, shut down earlier this year. Atlanta Civic Circle did not receive its second $50,000 grant because it didn’t complete the first LION audit, Anglin noted. (Atlanta Civic Circle did not respond to my request for an interview, but executive director Saba Long wrote on LinkedIn in June that “the funding environment for local nonprofit journalism is extraordinarily difficult right now.”) Other recipients have merged or transformed since applying for the grant.2.

    Industry observers note that RELATED ARTICLEFrom bad to worse: 2026 is shaping up to be “a super El Niño year for local news”Sophie CulpepperOctober 13, 2026Medill’s annual State of Local News report, released this month, describes a local news ecosystem in a “state of precarity.” That state of precariousness helps explain how $100,000 over two years can be a “godsend,” a “miracle,” and not enough. As one grantee put it, “Right now, these are shanties built on a beach, waiting for a hurricane to come through.”.

    According to recent reports, “Press Forward reached newsrooms that don’t have existing relationships with major national funders,” noted Nina Ignaczak, the founder, publisher, and editor of Planet Detroit. “The challenge now is whether the commitment holds.”.

    The funding helped newsrooms keep the lights on, whether they used it to pay bills, pay down debt, make payroll, or as a buffer when something went wrong.

    “The flexibility that Press Forward has given us has allowed us to fill — I wouldn’t say emergencies, but unexpected gaps,” said Richard Young, founder and executive director of CivicLex in Kentucky. It brought on a consulting editor to keep city hall coverage going after losing a reporter, and purchased fresh software. Without the funding, CivicLex likely would have had to dip into its reserves, he said.

    Bob Bonnar, publisher of the News Letter Journal in Wyoming, used the first payment from Press Forward to upgrade computers and cameras and give some staffers raises. “That chewed up the money very swiftly,” he noted, “and I probably should have held some of it back because the News Letter Journal ended up having a pretty rough year in 2025.” He had to use about half of the second $50,000 payment to repay an operating loan. The rest covered the remaining revenue shortfall and kept the organization in the black through the winter.

    Vandana Kumar, publisher of the California-based ethnic media outlet India Currents, described the funding as a “stabilizing force” that allowed the newsroom to keep operating despite a contraction in philanthropic giving and cuts to local government advertising.

    In a recent development, the Copper River Record built infrastructure to host digital ads and created a new website. It held listening sessions with Native villages in its coverage area and donated subscriptions to local Tribal offices. It improved the design of its print newspaper. Sayer paid freelancers to complete Press Pass training and pursued other professional development. And she was able to take on more ambitious stories about PFAS and “forever chemicals.”.

    Industry observers note that the Press Forward funding was “the biggest single windfall in nearly 20 years for our small community newspaper,” Sandpoint Reader publisher Ben Olson told me. The Idaho-based paper used the money to travel to the state capital for Press Club awards and design a newly introduced media kit, which Olson noted has improved ad sales. The Reader also paid a large chunk of its printing bill, paid its rent a year in advance, and gave staffers bonuses. (The bonuses helped the paper become 100% employee-owned; Olson’s two employees bought in when Olson’s business partner and co-owner retired.).

    It has been revealed that the open-ended nature of the grants gave Colorado’s World Journal “the flexibility to be able to make a change, do a thing, and then pivot as needed,” Sporleder Orr mentioned. “When we were in the toilet, all I could think about was, like, ‘Is there going to be anything in the post office today so that I can make payroll?’ ‘Oh, my God, we’ve got to pay rent.’” Sometimes she and her husband skipped their own paychecks to pay staff. The grant gave them “emotional bandwidth” to plan ahead.

    Many grantees used the funding to hire full- or part-time staffers. Sometimes, that worked out well.

    The Mānoa Mirror, an online newsroom based at the University of Hawaii at Mānoa, received two $25,000 grants, which it used to hire a managing editor, a student editorial coordinator, three student reporters, and a social media producer. (The managing editor was paid a stipend, and the other positions were part-time.) The work had previously depended on “faculty goodwill and volunteerism, which was not sustainable for long,” noted Hye-ryeon Lee, who was professor and chair of the school of communication and information until retiring this summer. With the new hires, the site went from publishing a few stories a month to publishing daily.

    Recent findings suggest that the Real WV’s first LION audit pointed to a need its small team had already recognized: hiring someone to sell ads. It hired a public school teacher with sales experience (including selling ads for the yearbook) part-time.

    The funding allowed Te Lo Cuento News to pay contributors consistently and to add contract, part-time positions including a sales manager, an office administrator, and a couple of reporters. The only position it could sustain beyond the grant period is the part-time sales manager, Ramírez Braiz stated.

    The Texas Spur is one of five weekly newspapers owned by Paragraph Ranch Media. Originally, the team planned to use the Press Forward grant to secure a loan to improve company housing and hire a journalist based in Spur (population 863 as of 2020). But nobody took the newspaper up on the free housing offer, said editor and general manager Barbara Brannon. So the company hired four early-career journalists (two full-time, two part-time) living in its 10-county coverage area. Three of the four left for jobs in other industries halfway through their second year. The one who stayed is doing well as a regional sports reporter, Brannon said, and a hire who replaced a person who left is now managing editor for The Post Dispatch.3.

    It has been revealed that the turnover Brannon experienced isn’t unique to Spur. Other newsrooms also found hiring with grant money challenging.

    Sometimes, that was because of location. “Had we been able to find the right people from the outset, I believe the grant would have had a greater impact on the business,” remarked Anton Kaufer, regional publisher for Hagadone Media Montana. In rural Northwest Montana, though, recruiting and retaining staff is a challenge, and Hagadone’s Mineral Independent struggled to replace its salesperson and office manager after they retired. The experience “reinforced for us that sustainability isn’t just about having the funding,” Kaufer said. “It’s also about having the people in place to make the most of it.”.

    Recent findings suggest that the World Journal tried placing an ad for a salesperson with the Colorado Press Association and got “absolutely no interest,” Sporleder Orr said. “People living in northern Colorado don’t particularly want to come live in a teeny-tiny town in a rural, broke part of the state.” (She credited the grant with giving her the mental space to fire a salesperson who wasn’t working out, then regroup.).

    Other times, the money just wasn’t enough. “The reality is that $100,000 over two years isn’t a lot,” one grantee who asked to stay anonymous told me. “You can’t hire somebody with that.”.

    It has been revealed that ecoRI’s experience illustrates those limitations. Before receiving the Press Forward grant, EcoRI had used other grant funding and reserves to hire a director of development in a one-year contract position. In its grant application to Press Forward, the team proposed converting that role into a full-time staff position with benefits.

    The salary limited the hiring pool, though. The development director position paid $65,000 a year, which “is really not the market rate for a director of development” in the area, publisher and cofounder Jo Detz noted. (She said it should be more like $90,000.) The staffer they ended up hiring came from another state and hadn’t worked in news before. In a staff position, he cost more than he was bringing in. Detz laid him off and eliminated the position last December. She called the experience “heartbreaking.”.

    “At the point where I knew this wasn’t working,” she noted, “there wasn’t enough runway to pivot, rethink, rehire.”.

    It has been revealed that beyond the salary limitations, Detz thinks the development director didn’t have enough runway to succeed. The kind of development the staffer was hired to oversee — major gifts and individual giving — is a long game; “that position would need at least two or three years to begin to see some benefits,” she noted. Now, she’s back where she started, juggling fundraising with her other work.

    “I know it’s crazy to say that $100,000 over two years wasn’t enough,” she stated, “but it was not enough to make a meaningful difference to our revenue strategy.”.

    In a recent development, planet Detroit’s Ignaczak was in a unique position: Around the same time the newsroom received the Press Forward grant, Planet Detroit also received a $500,000 three-year grant from the MacArthur Foundation. That grant allowed her to hire a managing editor, she stated.

    Ignaczak believes general operating support is what small nonprofit newsrooms need. But to be effective, “I really think fully funding a revenue role for a minimum of three years is what needs to happen to build sustainability, if that is the goal,” she said. “And $100,000 over two years is not enough to achieve that.”.

    In a recent development, notiVisión Georgia, a Spanish-language local news outlet with one full-time staffer, is committed to print in a world moving away from it. The print newspaper is the only way the outlet has been able to use to “generate real economic value,” said CEO Mónica Pirela, because it’s where local companies want to place ads. The organization spent some of its Press Forward funds on printing and distribution. Pirela wears “every hat” right now, and the organization’s top need is a dedicated sales manager, she said.

    Industry observers note that california’s BenitoLink, meanwhile, used some of the Press Forward funding to begin printing in 2025. That will allow it to apply for newspaper of record status and get paid for running legal notices.

    In a recent development, in Minnesota, Swift County Monitor-News publisher and owner Reed Anfinson called the grant a “godsend” at a time when tariffs and rising gas prices have driven up printing and delivery costs and weakened advertisers’ budgets. The for-profit Monitor-News put some of its Press Forward funding toward redesigning its print newspaper. Anfinson also purchased materials as part of an “Out of Sight/Out of Mind” advertising campaign stressing the value of print. (He created the campaign himself, using Midjourney for the images.) For news organizations in small towns, Anfinson believes, digital revenue will never be enough to sustain operations.

    Some organizations used the funding to expand their remit beyond news.

    In a recent development, for instance, the Copper River Record partnered with the Copper River Native Association to include weekly language graphics in the paper for Ahtna, a critically endangered language, coordinating with a local kindergarten class. That project required a lot of time and investment up front, Sayer mentioned, but it can continue beyond the life of the grant.

    Planet Detroit used some Press Forward funding for reporting, but “the most significant thing the grant made possible wasn’t any single story,” Ignaczak said. The grant gave the team time to work on its Civic Action Toolbox, which turns reporting into civic engagement prompts. In a story about a local ballot proposal, for instance, the embedded toolbox flags upcoming public meetings, links to contact information for local representatives, and suggests an organization to follow. The tool is also in beta testing with other newsrooms.

    “The whole project came from having the space to ask what our readers actually need from us beyond information, and then building toward that,” Ignaczak noted. “Unrestricted funding makes that kind of work possible.”.

    Sources indicate that anfinson of the Monitor-News took the unusual step of writing a grant application on behalf of the local school district, which was losing students to adjacent districts. He used some of the Press Forward funding to match a $2,500 grant to the district. The district then ran $5,000 in ads in a “goodwill effort” to stem declining enrollment. The partnership helped to raise the Monitor-News’s profile, he said, by highlighting the benefits of newspaper advertising.

    Press Forward required grantees to complete two LION sustainability audits. But it also offered optional coaching via the media consulting organization Blue Engine to help implement the first audit’s recommendations. Of the 205 grantees, 154 participated in coaching, Anglin said.

    Industry observers note that the coaching kicked off in January, with most individual coaches and grantees meeting monthly. Multiple participants said the support would have been more beneficial if it were introduced earlier. This was a tradeoff of Press Forward moving quickly to get money out the door, Anglin said.4.

    This was the first large, unrestricted grant Austin Common had ever received, and it struggled with how to spend the money. “It felt like a lot of pressure,” said Amy Stansbury, the site’s editor-in-chief and only full-time staffer.

    Stansbury wanted to bring on the organization’s first full-time employees, but didn’t want to make those hires (and spend all the grant money) until she had a clear initiative. The coaching helped her figure out which hires made the most strategic sense and how to budget for them.

    According to recent reports, A few publishers were lukewarm about the substance of the coaching, but the majority I heard from were enthusiastic. At first, Baldwin was skeptical and worried the coaching might amount to “checking a box.” In practice, though, he noted it’s been “tremendously helpful” for tasks like writing the job description for the Real WV’s sales position.

    Sporleder Orr called the coaching “incredible.” The monthly sessions helped her with everything from tackling grant proposals to improving her Google Analytics skills. The combination of money and coaching, she added, “makes sure that the recipients don’t just continue doing business as usual.”.

    It has been revealed that in addition to the funding, Press Forward paid for grantees to attend conferences. Anglin noted 111 grantees attended the Lenfest News Philanthropy Summit in Philadelphia in 2025, 81 attended the same conference (which I also attended) in 2026, and 87 attended the Business of Local conference in Salt Lake City in 2025. A handful of grantees attended affinity conferences.

    In a recent development, stansbury found attending conferences for the first time helpful and eye-opening. It taught her “there’s this secret shadow world of [invitation-only] foundation and grant funding.” Press Forward’s travel support to attend a national conference was “transformative” for India Currents, Kumar stated, giving it visibility and access to relationship-building.

    To small newsrooms, the grant felt like a Press Forward stamp of approval that put them on the map for other funders. The Mirror’s Lee called the Press Forward funding “instrumental” in securing a $20,000 grant from a local foundation. But that was an exception among publishers I heard from; most didn’t feel the visibility and credibility conferred by the grant directly translated to other funders giving them more money.

    According to recent reports, so several publishers, including Ramírez Braiz of Te Lo Cuento News, would like to see Press Forward go a step further and make individual introductions to funders. “Those more personal introductions can make a major difference for small organizations,” she stated.

    Ramírez Braiz also called for “more shared learning around outcomes and impact.” Few grantees had a good sense of what others in the cohort were up to, and some were interested in more knowledge sharing with peer organizations, though the day-to-day grind of keeping one’s own newsroom running was a common impediment.

    Since 2023, Anglin said, Press Forward’s network of more than 130 funders has invested $258 million directly in newsrooms. That suggests that over half of the more than $400 million the coalition indicates it’s invested has gone to newsrooms.

    Sources indicate that when Press Forward first declared the direct funding for newsrooms, it “felt really awesome,” the grantee who asked to stay anonymous told me. To the grantee, it was meaningful to see Press Forward give funding to more organizations than planned in response to the scale of need. But when Press Forward went on to a second funding round in which single organizations, including both newsrooms and newsroom-adjacent organizations like the International Women’s Media Foundation and LION, received as much as $1.5 million for infrastructure projects, the same grantee said it felt like “a slap in the face.”.

    According to recent reports, “Many of the problems newsrooms face aren’t unique to them individually,” Anglin said. “If we are attempting to solve problems at scale, we have to intervene not just at the newsroom level, but at the systems level, too.” She said that because many of the infrastructure grantees serve multiple newsrooms, “investing in them creates a multiplier effect across the industry.”.

    Industry observers note that the argument that funding support organizations and infrastructure lifts more boats is “a cop-out,” this publisher stated. “I think the philanthropists know it, I think the associations know it, and I think the potential grantees that are not funders or associations or intermediaries know it.”.

    Young had a different perspective. Because of CivicLex’s broad scope, it seeks out funding from both democracy funders and journalism funders. Young thinks local news funders are way ahead on getting dollars into local communities.

    “I think Press Forward has done one of the more effective jobs of anything I’ve seen in the broader landscape of my world, and the civic renewal space, of delivering resources to the local level,” he stated. (He added, “No one is ever happy in the local news ecosystem when I say that folks in the local news ecosystem don’t know how good they have it. That does not win me a lot of friends.”).

    Most publishers I heard from see grants like this as critical to continued operation, yet they’re wary of overreliance on philanthropy.

    Industry observers note that young said he’d be surprised if local news is still a focus for national philanthropy in eight years. “Filling your cup up with money that will be impossible to recover in four years is a danger zone,” he added.

    Right now, more than 80% of Planet Detroit’s revenue mix comes from foundations. Ignaczak noted the organization hopes to bring that down to 50% by 2028. “But for nonprofit newsrooms covering environmental and public health problems in a mid-size metro, general operating grants aren’t a crutch,” she said. “They’re infrastructure.”.

    As for Press Forward, “Time will tell, as these grants go away, what impact [they’ve] actually had on the newsrooms that received [them], how many have managed to build sustainability,” she added. “I think a newsroom that needed $50,000 to survive to next year had problems that $50,000 isn’t going to solve.”.

    In a recent development, LOOKOUT executive director Jake Hylton believes there’s enough funding to go around. “While there may not be enough to support every single newsroom at a very large amount,” he stated, “I do believe that there is a larger investment in news that could be done.”.

    Sources indicate that A second grantee who asked to stay anonymous was blunt about their fears for the future. “We’re scared shitless about 2027,” this person mentioned, “because not only is the Press Forward money not returning, we also see none of the national grants that sustained us in 2024 and previous years.”.

    According to recent reports, the Copper River Record was in the black before receiving this grant, and the lean paper’s fixed overhead remains low. For the Record, Press Forward has been like “a fairy godmother,” Sayer stated.

    It has been revealed that “I’m not going to lie: I will miss having the money to say yes to any reasonable story,” she continued. “But I think that, even going back to our original budget, the strength of what we learned will continue to help us deliver a higher quality paper that is more relevant to the communities we serve.”.

    Recent findings suggest that the Sandpoint Reader, Olson said, is “surviving” right now. “We’d love to be thriving,” he added, “but we’re happy to continue to survive when many print publications aren’t.” He credited the Press Forward grant with giving the burned-out team “the chance to fall in love with our industry again.”.

    Sporleder Orr feels nervous about what’s ahead, but with the World Journal in a much more comfortable cash flow position, she and her husband are “in a way better mental state about the business.”.

    “We feel good about the future right now, that we are going to be able to keep going and make it,” she said. “We’re back to, ‘This is what we do ’til we die.'”.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    CloudLinux is the maker of Imunify360 — a suite of security products protecting millions of websites across the web hosting industry — and of CloudLinux OS, the operating system behind a large share of the world's shared hosting. To learn more about our company and products, visit our websites: cloudlinux.com and imunify360.com. Alongside those established product lines we run a small innovation team whose job is to find and prove the next ones.

    In a recent development, we are looking for a Product Owner to lead that team: a small, senior, fully remote squad of engineers that takes new product concepts from idea to a working MVP in customers' hands, then hands proven products to a product line and moves on to the next concept. You will be accountable for the pipeline of ideas, the speed and rigour with which they are tested, and the evidence behind every go / no-go recommendation.

    It has been revealed that this is a hands-on lead role, not pure people management: roughly 50% discovery and leadership (customer conversations, scoping, prioritisation, coaching, reporting to the CPO) and 50% building (prototypes, spikes, design and code review, demo stands). You will not be the team's only builder, but you must be able to build a credible prototype yourself and hold a technical opinion about every part of it.

    According to recent reports, you don't need to arrive as an expert in web hosting or security. If you have taken a product from nothing to its first paying customers before — as a founder, an early engineer, or the lead of an incubation team — and you get deep into unfamiliar technical territory fast, we will teach you the market.

    It has been revealed that the innovation team sits across CloudLinux and Imunify and owns the product concepts that do not yet have a home in an established product line. Ideas come from customer conversations, industry events, telemetry across more than 80,000 servers and the CPO’s strategy; the team’s job is to turn them into something a customer will pay for within a quarter, using AI coding agents throughout.

    Prototyping and technical direction.

    We evaluate engineers partly on how effectively they work with coding agents, and in the innovation team this is the main lever on speed. As the lead you model and coach it: prompt specificity, review quality on agent-generated code, context provision, iteration and error recovery, and end-to-end task completion. Expect to use agents to build prototypes, generate test corpora and draft customer-facing material.

    #112754. Tech Report: Elon Musk’s Grokipedia is littered with mistakes. But Wikipedia could still learn some things from it.

    📖 Baca

    Tech Report: Elon Musk’s Grokipedia is littered with mistakes. But Wikipedia could still learn some things from it.

    📅 02 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 26 min read (5145 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Niemanlab

    ⏱️ ~26 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, all the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing.
    • Industry observers note that we will never sell your address.
    • Recent findings suggest that we have sent a confirmation link to .
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, all the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    Industry observers note that we will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

    Nearly there — check your email.

    Recent findings suggest that we have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

    Grokipedia demonstrates that AI is actually pretty good at finding tidbits in the far corners of the internet.

    Industry observers note that when I saw Grokipedia’s articles about me, the memories came rushing back: my 19 years in minor league baseball, including that impressive season with the Montgomery Rebels when I hit 20 home runs. I was lean back then — 6 feet tall and 168 pounds — and earned a career batting average just under .300. I became a minor league coach and managed the Chicago White Sox for a short stint in 1970, which Grokipedia remarked “highlighted [my] readiness for higher-level responsibilities.”.

    I then attended Arizona State University, switched to a career in journalism, created the fact-checking site PolitiFact, won a Pulitzer Prize, and now teach journalism at Duke University.

    According to recent reports, ah, the memories!…except that I never played minor league baseball, never managed the White Sox, and can only dream about being 6 feet tall. (I’m 5’8″.) Grokipedia, the AI-written encyclopedia of Elon Musk, has confused me with Marion Danne “Bill” Adair, who died in 2002.

    In a recent development, that article and another one about “Bill Adair (journalist)” — which really is me — illustrate the many flaws of Grokipedia, which launched a year ago. The articles are littered with mistakes and superfluous details. They are terribly written and ridiculously long. If Grok, the AI engine that wrote this turgid prose, were a student in one of my writing courses, I would give it a D. (Editor’s note: After this article was published, someone updated the inaccurate Grok pages. The original versions are linked here.).

    According to recent reports, still, the articles provide valuable lessons for Wikipedia editors who are debating how and when to use AI. Grokipedia adds fresh content and context that Wikipedia often lacks. It shows that AI is actually pretty good at finding tidbits in the far corners of the internet and summarizing them in sweeping prose. It can also provide balance to articles that need it.

    Grok can’t write worth a lick, but it shows how Wikipedia can take advantage of AI at a time when overworked editors are trying to keep the encyclopedia alive.

    According to recent reports, musk rolled out Grokipedia as an alternative to Wikipedia, which he said was too liberal. (He called it “Wokepedia.”) Still, he trusted it enough to have Grok copy hundreds of thousands of its articles, which is permitted under Wikipedia’s Creative Commons license, and then add content from elsewhere on the internet. With his usual bluster, Musk said his encyclopedia used a newly introduced version of his large language model that was good at “cogent analysis.” He said programmers told it to “cycle through the million most popular articles in Wikipedia and add, modify, and delete.” When Grokipedia launched, Musk said he had substantial aspirations to overtake Wikipedia, which has 68 million articles in more than 300 languages. He said his encyclopedia would be more complete and more balanced and would make smarter use of images and video. Maybe someday. For now, Grokipedia is a massive collection of overly long articles that are often out of date. Its flaws have been well-documented: Articles are littered with mistakes, peddle conspiracy theories, rely on low-credibility sources, and sometimes skew to the right. And although Grokipedia demonstrates edit requests from readers and whether they are approved, the site is not as transparent as Wikipedia, which reveals details about its editors and every change they make. Last spring, Grokipedia mysteriously stopped updating, according to a report by researchers Renée DiResta and Ronald Robertson. It resumed in late September, still a hot mess, but with a more colorful homepage that always seems to feature its article about Musk. Grokipedia has two articles about me: the conflated baseball player one and “Bill Adair (journalist),” the real one, which is incredibly boring, even to me. Both borrow heavily from Wikipedia’s articles about us and enrich them with details found on assorted websites. Wikipedia’s article about me is nicely concise — just 700 words. It is written in the encyclopedia’s signature dry style and doesn’t contain any errors. The article recounts my career, some of the major news events I’ve covered, the two books I’ve written, and the awards I’ve won. But it highlights trivial events from my career, fails to emphasize larger ones, and lacks any criticism of my work. (I have not tried to improve the article because Wikipedia’s conflict of interest policy prohibits people from editing their own bios.) By contrast, Grokipedia’s “Bill Adair (journalist)” is painfully long — 5,600 words. Its greatest value would be to help someone suffering from a sleep disorder. Like a college student trying to meet a word count, Grok stuffed the article with needless details and redundant descriptions. The article tells you about my work with PolitiFact and then tells you again and again. It explains the site’s rating scale eight times and mentions my academic title four times. Despite labels that say “fact-checked by Grok,” both articles had lots of errors. I spotted 32 in the journalist one and so many in the baseball mashup that I couldn’t count them all. Mistakes are not surprising in AI writing, but I discovered interesting patterns that reveal the weaknesses of large language models. In the article about the real me, only seven of the errors were hallucinations in which Grok seemed to create a detail out of thin air. No, I did not win an award from Manhattan College, and no, PolitiFact did not begin by fact-checking the Tampa mayor’s race. Five other errors showed Grok was a lazy researcher that did not look broadly enough to check a claim. Grok said I am the director of Duke’s journalism program, but I left that job five years ago. The sources cited in the article don’t explain Grok’s mistake, so it seems likely it remembered an old announcement and failed to see a newer one that named my successor. The most prevalent errors were in a broad category I’d all cluelessness. These mistakes showed Grok didn’t fully understand what it read, like someone who skimmed an article too quickly. My favorite in this category was when I got credit for a big scoop in 2000 that George W. Bush had a DUI conviction, which the Grokipedia article said had an impact on “late-election discourse.” I wish! Yes, I was among the many journalists who covered that story, but I had no scoop. Together, the errors reveal that Grok is a knucklehead. It doesn’t know what’s vital and what’s not. It is simply mashing together details from many web articles about me. Grok only knows what it found on the internet and it lacks experience and perspective to sort out what’s important. The writing is dreadful. The articles read as if Grok was trained on too many online resumes and corporate memos. Grok uses words and phrases like “commenced” and “transitioned” and “multidisciplinary practicum” and “hypotheses on fact-check efficacy.” A typical sentence: “Adair’s approach in this position reflected a commitment to undiluted sourcing and causal analysis of policy impacts, influencing subsequent innovations in political journalism.” Take a close look at that sentence and you’ll see it’s just a mush of buzzwords. I don’t know what “undiluted sourcing” is and have never used the phrase, nor would I refer to “causal analysis”…of anything. Grok is trying to impress us with an MBA vocabulary but is really just an epic bullshitter. Bernadette Meehan, CEO of the Wikimedia Foundation, which provides money and technical infrastructure for the encyclopedia, has called AI “an existential threat” to Wikipedia. The 25-year-old encyclopedia has long been a source and beneficiary of Google searches. Wikipedia provides the answers and in turn benefits from readers clicking through to read articles. But when people make a query to a chatbot, they often get the answer they need in an AI summary and don’t click through to read the encyclopedia article. That threatens donations because fewer readers see Wikipedia’s fundraising pitches. Wikipedia has banned content generated by LLMs, but that hasn’t stopped many contributors — some well-intentioned, some not — from dumping an avalanche of AI-written content on the site. That has put a huge burden on the site’s “New pages patrol,” the editors who approve articles, because they must weed out the lousy content. (Wikipedia has a helpful guide of LLMs’ favorite words and phrases, such as “tapestry” and “meticulously” and sentences that start with “additionally.”) Still, terrible as it is, Grokipedia offers lessons in how AI can help Wikipedia. Grok’s voracious internet searches sometimes find things that human editors don’t. The long article about me includes a substantive discussion of my research about lying in politics and my work with fact-checkers around the world, neither of which are in the Wikipedia version. Grokipedia also provides some welcome balance. When it offers context, Grokipedia can be a little heavy with hype (“His work has been lauded for innovating transparency in media…”) But it also included a “Criticisms and Controversies” section that details complaints that PolitiFact is biased against Republicans. That section has a healthy back and forth about the critiques and my response. That kind of balance could be helpful for Wikipedia, which has taken heat from Musk and others for being too lefty. Musk’s encyclopedia also has a playful spirit that Wikipedia could learn from. Grokipedia’s homepage features random samples of recent edits that provide a glimpse at how the site is being improved. Another Grokipedia feature reads articles aloud in an AI voice you select: Eve, who sounds like a BBC anchor; Ara, a serious woman with crisp diction; Leo, who might have been a professor at Oxford; and Sal, whose name suggests a sports bar but whose voice is NPR. My big takeaway from Grok is the importance of human judgment in curating knowledge. Grok is a bot trying to behave like a human editor. Its many mistakes and lousy writing show that AI is not ready to replace Wikipedia’s talented volunteers. Still, Grok shows that AI can be a tool that helps them research and write better articles. After seeing an AI encyclopedia up close through my experiences with Grok, I come away with hope. Yes, AI can be a sloppy researcher and an awful writer. But Grok’s performance, shaky as it was, highlighted AI’s readiness for higher-level responsibilities. Bill Adair, the Knight Professor of the Practice of Journalism and Public Policy at Duke University, is writing a book about how Wikipedia editors are adapting to the age of AI.

    Sources indicate that musk rolled out Grokipedia as an alternative to Wikipedia, which he noted was too liberal. (He called it “Wokepedia.”) Still, he trusted it enough to have Grok copy hundreds of thousands of its articles, which is permitted under Wikipedia’s Creative Commons license, and then add content from elsewhere on the internet.

    With his usual bluster, Musk said his encyclopedia used a new version of his large language model that was good at “cogent analysis.” He said programmers told it to “cycle through the million most popular articles in Wikipedia and add, modify, and delete.”.

    When Grokipedia launched, Musk mentioned he had massive aspirations to overtake Wikipedia, which has 68 million articles in more than 300 languages. He said his encyclopedia would be more complete and more balanced and would make smarter use of images and video.

    According to recent reports, for now, Grokipedia is a massive collection of overly long articles that are often out of date. Its flaws have been well-documented: Articles are littered with mistakes, peddle conspiracy theories, rely on low-credibility sources, and sometimes skew to the right. And although Grokipedia reveals edit requests from readers and whether they are approved, the site is not as transparent as Wikipedia, which reveals details about its editors and every change they make.

    It has been revealed that last spring, Grokipedia mysteriously stopped updating, according to a report by researchers Renée DiResta and Ronald Robertson. It resumed in late September, still a hot mess, but with a more colorful homepage that always seems to feature its article about Musk.

    According to recent reports, right now, if you don’t want your site to be scraped by AI companies, you have to block each organization’s crawlers individually. On Friday, Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, and Microsoft mentioned they would support a common robots.txt signal that, per OpenAI, “makes it easier for publishers and website operators to communicate the same preference to multiple participating providers at once.”.

    Anthropic engineer Kevin Kelley proposed the common signal as part of work for the Internet Engineering Task Force, and Anthropic is already supporting it. OpenAI states it will do so “in the coming months,” and Google and Microsoft say they’ll do so next year.

    Meta VP of communications Andy Stone called the common signal “an notable step,” writing in a tweet that the firm supports “publishers’ ability to express preferences about how their content is used for foundational generative AI training.” Meta is under scrutiny for proposed commercial terms that would allow broad scraping; last week, it agreed to delay implementation of those terms.

    It has been revealed that you’ll take ownership of customer billing inquiries across EMEA, partnering directly with customers and working cross-functionally with our Billing Engineering team. Beyond resolving complications, you’ll help identify patterns, improve workflows, and contribute to product enhancements that scale.

    This role is ideal for someone who thrives in async, fast-paced environments and is excited about helping millions of customers.

    Provide initial and timely responses to all support cases for a variety of topics, from billing or pre-sales requests to usage optimization or disputes.

    Debug/Identify user-specific challenges such as failed payments, unsettled invoices, payment extensions.

    Triage support cases including directing users to previous answers, code examples, documentation, or escalating to specific technical or business team members.

    Identify where internal tooling might be developed or obtained to improve support efficiency.

    Reproduce complications, create test cases and improve test coverage, if you have experience with testing.

    Experienced in customer support, with 2+ years of experience providing billing support to technical customers.

    Excellent communication skills and fluency in English.

    Communicate clearly across both technical and non-technical audiences.

    Have experience in async or globally distributed teams.

    Are comfortable navigating ambiguity and moving rapidly.

    Being proficient in SQL is a bonus.

    In a recent development, we hire globally. We believe you can do your best work from anywhere. There are no Supabase offices, but we provide a WeWork membership or co-working allowance you can use anywhere in the world.

    Every team member receives ESOP (equity ownership) in the manufacturer. We want everyone to share in the upside of what we’re building together.

    Use this budget to set up your ideal work environment—laptop, monitor, headphones, or whatever helps you do your best work.

    Supabase covers 100% of health insurance for employees and 80% for dependents, wherever you are. Your wellbeing and your family’s health are important to us.

    Recent findings suggest that once a year, the entire manufacturer gathers in a new city for a week of connection, collaboration, and fun. It’s a highlight of our year.

    According to recent reports, we operate asynchronously and trust you to manage your own time. You know what needs to be done and when.

    Every team member receives an annual education allowance to spend on learning—courses, books, conferences, or anything that supports your growth.

    Supabase was born-remote and open-source-first. We believe our globally distributed team is our secret weapon in building tools developers love.

    Over $1B raised (including our $500M Series F).

    We move fast, build in public, and use what we ship. If it’s in your project, we probably use it in ours too. We believe deeply in the open-source ecosystem and strive to support—not replace—existing tools and communities.

    Recent findings suggest that camunda is the enterprise platform for agentic orchestration, enabling organizations to coordinate AI agents, people, and systems across complex, end-to-end business processes. With built-in governance, auditability, and human oversight, Camunda gives enterprises the control they need to move AI from pilots to production — safely and at scale. Trusted by over 700 organizations worldwide, including 9 of top 10 US banks, Camunda helps enterprises boost operational efficiency, accelerate time-to-value, and deliver better customer experiences.Fully remote and global, we are in the middle of something bigger: transforming into an AI-first organisation, built on our own platform. We use Agentic AI to automate, orchestrate intelligent processes, and elevate human contribution across every team.Named GP Bullhound’s Top 100 Next Unicorn list, 2025 Great Place to Work certified. Visionary in 2025 Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ for Business Orchestration and Automation Technologies. ranked 3rd in Flexa's 2026 Most Flexible Companies, We’re growing fast and looking for top talent to join our team. If you want meaningful work, visible impact and put something genuinely rare on your CV, keep reading.

    Industry observers note that we run Camunda on Camunda. Our Enterprise Agentic Automation Team (EAAT) builds production-grade agentic orchestration using Camunda's platform for Camunda's own operations, from Finance to Support to Go-to-Market. As Senior Architect, you own delivery on our EAAT-led initiatives end to end. You partner with process owners to uncover where the biggest value lies, redesign how the work should flow, decide where agents, rules or people handle each step, and shape it into scope our engineers can build from directly. Then you lead technical delivery management with our engineers, steering increments, dependencies and decisions until you get it live and prove the value. You won't design and hand over: you stay until it works in production, and keep evolving it.

    Own delivery of our use cases end to end, business and technical, from discovery to production and value realization.

    Run discovery with process owners: as-is baseline, target process, and where agents, rules or humans handle each step.

    Turn target processes into epics engineers can build from directly: scenarios, acceptance criteria, increments.

    Design solutions within our reference architecture, and bring new patterns based on lessons learned.

    Lead technical delivery on your initiatives: plan increments with the engineers, manage dependencies and risks, and keep process owners and sponsors aligned on progress and decisions.

    Define and track value per initiative and increment, and keep business decisions moving.

    Feed delivery learnings back into the reference architecture, our delivery method and Camunda's product.

    Ability and/or willingness to use our product.

    7+ years in solution architecture or technical/process consulting, with an engineering background (Java, JavaScript or similar) and significant time delivering for the business or customers.

    A track record of leading process orchestration initiatives (Camunda or comparable) from discovery to production, not just designing them and handing over.

    Strong business analysis and process management skills: runs discovery and process redesign workshops with business stakeholders, models processes in BPMN, and turns the outcome into solid solution designs.

    Solution and data architecture in an enterprise context: integrations and APIs, and the data a process and its agents need across systems.

    An AI-first mindset, including first experience designing and building enterprise-grade agentic solutions.

    Holds their own with senior stakeholders and gets decisions made.

    Experience in Finance or other back-office process domains and operations (P2P, Q2C).

    Experience with process intelligence or mining tools.

    Working knowledge of enterprise systems such as NetSuite, Salesforce or Zip.
